paras: The lynching of William Parish was the killing of a prisoner by masked men in Newellton, Tensas Parish, Louisiana, on a Friday night in late February or March 1882. Parish, accused of shooting Sol. Waters over a deer skin, was taken from his chain and hanged in town. A coroner's jury found he died by strangulation at the hands of men unknown.

According to the North Louisiana Journal, Waters and Parish quarreled on Monday, February 20, over a deer skin. As Waters stooped to cut the skin in half with his razor, Parish was said to have seized Waters' shotgun and shot him in the back with fifteen buckshot. The Journal reported that Parish said he cared no more about killing "a negro or a white man" than about eating his dinner, and that his punishment would only be levee work. Neither account states the race of Parish or Waters.

Parish was afterward held chained to a tree in the yard of Captain S. D. S. Newell's former residence in Newellton; who held him is not said. Between 2 and 3 a.m. on a Friday, "about fifteen or twenty" masked men seized him and stuffed his mouth with cotton. They hanged him from a tree in front of Dr. Percy's office in Newellton, though the Journal heard he was strangled first.
The coroner's jury found that Parish had died "by strangulation at the hands of men unknown to the jury." No report of arrests or of any further inquiry appears in the coverage.

The fullest account was a North Louisiana Journal item, reprinted on March 18 by the Lake Charles Echo under the headline "Murder and Lynch Law in Tansas Parish." The item dwelt on Parish's alleged crime and boast and offered no comment on the masked men. On April 15 the Donaldsonville Chief said in one sentence that Parish had "brutally murdered" Waters and was hanged by masked men. Because the Echo reprinted the Journal's "Friday last" without the Journal's issue date, the hanging can be placed only on a Friday between late February and March 17.

Fifteen or twenty masked men took Parish from where he was chained and hanged or strangled him, and the inquest found death 'at the hands of men unknown' (A1); the killing followed his alleged killing of Waters, a crime pretext (A1, A2).

The only full account is a North Louisiana Journal item reprinted in the Lake Charles Echo (A1); the Donaldsonville Chief brief (A2) agrees but adds nothing and cannot be shown to be independent of it.
